raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old male presented to us with acute increase in bilateral neck swelling since 5-6 days, neck pain, fever, and weight loss.
Patient had first noticed the swelling 2 months ago. It started as multiple neck swellings which were initially small. He did not take any treatment for it. Later on he was admitted for altered sensorium. His serology for HIV was positive andfine needle aspiration cytology of swelling was suggestive of tuberculosis. CD4 count was 48 cells/mm. Magnetic resonance imaging of brain was normal. He was given category 1(2HREZ+4HR) under RNTCP and Anti Retroviral antiretroviral therapy (3TC+d4T+EFV), with septran and fluconazole for prophylaxis against pneumocystis carinii and fungal infections. He improved symptomatically after the drugs were started, even though there was no appreciable change in the number and size of swelling.
After about 2 months of treatment there was acute aggravation of complaints for which the patient presented to us. There was a history of increase in size of swelling during the past 1 week. On examination of the neck swellings, there were multiple, discrete, firm, mobile, tender, nonwarm, nonreducible, nonpulsatile swellings on both sides of the neck involving all lymph node groups [Figure 1, 2]. The swellings were of different sizes ranging from 2 to 12 cm in maximum dimension. There was no enlargement of any other lymph node groups in the body. Ultrasonography of the neck revealed multiple bilateral enlarged conglomerated nodes in levels 2, 3, 4, and 5. Chest X ray was normal. Sputum examinations of two morning samples were negative for acid fast bacilli. CD4 count was 100 cells per cubic millimeter of blood.
At this stage considering the fact that in spite of treatment with ATT+ART, the patient had presented with increase in size of neck swelling, we were considering a differential diagnosis of infection with drug-resistant bacilli, infection by MOTT, and IRD.
Tablet prednisolone 25 mg once daily was added to his treatment and it was tapered over a period of 3 weeks. The swelling gradually became soft; skin over swelling became tense and red. About 100 cc pus was aspirated from neck swelling and sent for mycobacterial culture and sensitivity. AFB culture report (BACTEC/L-J) was suggestive of M. avium complex (MAC) on the basis of NAP (rho-nitro-alpha-acetyl amino-beta-hydroxy-propiophenone) and morphology. AFB culture and sensitivity report showed sensitive to all first line drugs. The patient had a diagnosis of AIDS, he was on antiretroviral therapy with increase in CD4 count and worsening of preexisting disease; hence, the diagnosis was IRD.
Along with category-1 ATT and ART, azithromycin and ciprofloxacin were added for MOTT. Patient was kept on fortnightly follow-up. At the time of sending this publication the patient had completed 4 months of treatment and the patient is symptomatically better with marked reduction in size of the swelling [Figure 3].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old HIV-positive male on anti-tuberculosis and antiretroviral therapy presented with a 5-to-6-day history of acute painful enlargement of bilateral neck swellings, fever, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient first noticed multiple small neck swellings 2 months prior to presentation, followed by an admission for altered sensorium where he was diagnosed with HIV infection (CD4 count 48 cells/mm3) and cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis by fine-needle aspiration cytology (with normal brain MRI). He was started on RNTCP Category I anti-tuberculosis therapy (2HREZ/4HR), antiretroviral therapy (lamivudine, stavudine, and efavirenz), cotrimoxazole, and fluconazole with initial symptomatic improvement. However, after 2 months of combined therapy, he experienced an acute 1-week flare of painful, rapidly enlarging bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, and weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection and cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis diagnosed 2 months prior (baseline CD4 count 48 cells/mm3; normal brain MRI).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for bilateral neck pain and swelling, fever, and weight loss. Home medications: lamivudine, stavudine, efavirenz, Category I ATT (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Septran), and fluconazole.

objective.physical_examination: Neck examination revealed multiple discrete, firm, mobile, tender, non-warm, non-reducible, non-pulsatile bilateral cervical lymph node enlargements involving all cervical nodal levels (measuring 2 to 12 cm in maximum dimension), which subsequently softened with overlying tense erythematous skin yielding ~100 mL of pus upon aspiration. No extra-cervical lymphadenopathy was present.
objective.routine_investigations: Two morning sputum samples were negative for acid-fast bacilli. Chest X-ray was normal. Neck ultrasonography demonstrated multiple bilateral enlarged conglomerated lymph nodes across cervical levels II, III, IV, and V.
objective.advanced_workup: Repeat CD4+ T-cell count had doubled from 48 cells/mm3 at baseline to 100 cells/mm3. Aspiration of ~100 mL of pus from the suppurative cervical lymph nodes with mycobacterial culture on BACTEC and Löwenstein-Jensen media identified Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC / MOTT) based on NAP test and colony morphology, with susceptibility to all first-line anti-TB drugs.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Paradoxical/unmasking mycobacterial immune reconstitution disease (IRD / IRIS) with Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC / MOTT) suppurative cervical lymphadenitis in a 35-year-old male with AIDS (CD4+ count rising from 48 to 100 cells/mm3 after 2 months of lamivudine/stavudine/efavirenz and Category I anti-tuberculosis therapy). Management included a 3-week tapering course of oral prednisolone (starting at 25 mg once daily), therapeutic pus aspiration (~100 mL), continuation of Category I ATT and ART, and addition of azithromycin and ciprofloxacin for MAC coverage, resulting in marked regression of the cervical lymphadenopathy and symptomatic recovery at 4-month follow-up.
